title: The Skinny on Lyme Disease
summary: Josh and Chuck explain Lyme disease: its bacterial cause (Borrelia burgdorferi, a spirochete), transmission by nymphal black-legged (deer) ticks that must stay attached roughly 24 to 36 hours, the erythema migrans bull's-eye rash, and why diagnosis is hard given delayed antibody response and short window for direct testing. They cover the history from the Lyme, Connecticut cluster of juvenile arthritis cases in the early 1970s, patient advocates Judith Mitchell and Polly Murray, Willy Burgdorfer's identification of the bacterium, and the debate over antibiotic treatment and post-treatment Lyme disease syndrome. They also discuss prevention (tucking pants into socks, tick checks, showering), a conspiracy theory linking Lyme to Cold War bioweapon research at Plum Island and Fort Detrick (from Chris Newby's book and Rep. Chris Smith's legislation), the climate change and deer-population explanations for the spread, and a listener mail story about tickets at a Maine show. Note the transcript spells the advocate's name 'Judith Minch'; the hosts' spelling of the bacterium is Borrelia burgdorferi.

entities.name: Bitten: The Secret History of Lyme Disease and Biological Weapons

segments.title: Tour dates, opening banter and Lyme disease overview
segments.summary: Tour dates in Orlando and New Orleans are announced. The hosts introduce Lyme disease, its name from the town, its rapid spread across the US, and the debate over its treatment and chronic symptoms.

segments.title: How Lyme is transmitted and its symptoms
segments.summary: Borrelia burgdorferi is transmitted by nymph ticks that must stay attached about 24 to 36 hours. The bacterium moves through the blood and attaches to blood vessel walls, and can change its surface proteins quickly to evade antibodies. Symptoms include fever, fatigue and the bull's-eye rash, and Ötzi the Iceman is mentioned as an ancient case.

segments.title: Lyme, Connecticut cluster and discovery of the bacterium
segments.summary: Children and adults in Lyme and Old Lyme, Connecticut had arthritis, rashes and fatigue in the early 1970s. Judith Mitchell and Polly Murray pushed for investigation, and the cluster reached Willy Burgdorfer, who identified the spirochete.

segments.title: Diagnosis, testing and antibiotic treatment debate
segments.summary: Early Lyme is usually treated with a short course of oral antibiotics, but diagnosis is hard because symptoms overlap with many conditions. Blood tests may be negative early, and direct bacterial tests have a brief window. Two-tier testing is advocated. Patients and advocates argue that short treatment courses may be insufficient, leading to post-treatment Lyme disease syndrome.

segments.title: Autoimmune theories and ongoing medical disagreement
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the possibility that Lyme leaves cell-wall remnants or triggers autoimmune responses that could lead to arthritis or heart problems. They note the disagreement between patient groups and the medical establishment, and that the epidemic scale is increasingly taken seriously.

segments.title: Tick prevention and checking for ticks
segments.summary: Advice includes tucking pants into socks, wearing light colors, checking the body and pets after walks, showering soon after, and removing adult ticks. Ticks found unattached are unlikely to transmit disease. Dog ticks are not the Lyme carriers.

segments.title: Plum Island bioweapon conspiracy theory
segments.summary: Chris Newby's book Bitten and Rep. Chris Smith's legislation claim that Cold War research at Fort Detrick and Plum Island used ticks as bioweapons and that the bacteria escaped near Lyme. The hosts find the theory implausible given Lyme's presence in multiple states and the difficulty of using ticks as a weapon, but note the Tick Act and its funding.

segments.title: Climate change, deer populations and wolves
segments.summary: The hosts discuss climate change as a reason for ticks surviving winters and spreading, the EPA using Lyme as a climate indicator, moose deaths from ticks, and deer population growth with the idea of reintroducing wolves.

segments.title: Listener mail: Old Orchard Beach show tickets
segments.summary: Listener Rich Clark describes getting third-row tickets at a Maine show from a stranger named Matt whose friends were stuck in traffic. The hosts thank Matt and the fans.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts encourage listeners to get in touch through the website or email and close the show.
